company.name: Orchard Payroll
company.one_liner: Payroll and compliance for agricultural employers

problem.statement: Agricultural payroll is piece-rate, seasonal, multi-jurisdiction and subject to H-2A rules. General payroll software cannot express it, so farm offices run spreadsheets alongside whatever they bought.
problem.who_has_it: Agricultural employers / farm offices (inferred from 'farm offices' and the deck title 'Payroll and compliance for agricultural employers')
evidence_given: No evidence offered beyond the assertion itself — no customer interviews, survey data, cited studies, or quantified cost of the spreadsheet workaround.
The only supporting detail is the descriptive list of payroll attributes (piece-rate, seasonal, multi-jurisdiction, H-2A).

solution.description: Piece-rate and hourly in one pay run, H-2A wage-rate compliance built in, and seasonal crew onboarding that survives a 400-person intake week.
solution.how_it_works: Not stated. The deck lists capabilities but gives no architecture, data model, integration, or implementation detail.
differentiators: Piece-rate and hourly handled in a single pay run
Seasonal crew onboarding at scale ('survives a 400-person intake week')

customer_segments: Agricultural employers / farms (210 farms are current customers)
Specialty crop growers (named as the expansion target in the ask, not a stated current segment)

business_model.acv_or_arpu: Not stated. Inferred only: $3.4M ARR across 210 farms implies roughly $16k average ARR per farm — this figure is derived by the analyst, not stated in the deck.

other_metrics: 'We win 7 of every 10 head-to-head evaluations' against AgriPay and HarvestHR (slide 4) — a competitive metric with no sample size or time period

competition.positioning_claim: The two vendors built for this market are AgriPay and HarvestHR. We win 7 of every 10 head-to-head evaluations against them. That win rate is the clearest evidence we have that the product is better.
competitors_omitted_suspicion: General-purpose payroll and HCM platforms are dismissed collectively on slide 2 as software that 'cannot express' ag payroll, but none is named or compared — despite being the incumbent that farm offices are described as already having 'bought.'
Farm-management and ag-ERP suites that bundle labor/payroll modules are not addressed at all.

Spreadsheets/manual process are described as the status quo on slide 2 but are never treated as a competitor in the competition slide — the deck frames the contest as a two-vendor bake-off while its own problem slide says the real alternative is spreadsheets plus incumbent software.
Regional payroll bureaus, PEOs, and H-2A labor contractors / agents who handle compliance as a service are not mentioned.

gtm.sales_motion: Not stated. The reference to 'head-to-head evaluations' implies a competitive, evaluated sales process (inference, not stated).

vague_language: 'expand into specialty crops' — no definition of which crops, geographies, or what expansion consists of
'seasonal crew onboarding that survives a 400-person intake week' — 'survives' is unquantified; no throughput, error-rate, or time-to-onboard metric
'General payroll software cannot express it' — 'cannot express' is rhetorical rather than a testable technical limitation
'the clearest evidence we have that the product is better' — 'better' is undefined and self-assessed
'The two vendors built for this market' — asserts the completeness of the competitive set without qualification
unsupported_numbers: '7 of every 10 head-to-head evaluations' — no sample size, no time window, no definition of what counts as a head-to-head evaluation or who recorded the outcome; self-reported win rates are typically drawn from a seller-selected subset of deals
'$3.4M ARR' — no definition of ARR (contracted vs. run-rate), no seasonality adjustment despite a business the deck itself describes as seasonal
'6% MoM growth for eight months' — no starting base, no statement of whether it is ARR or billings, and eight months of history in a seasonal market may capture only the harvest ramp

'Net revenue retention 108%' — no cohort definition, no measurement period, no gross retention/logo churn alongside it; in a seasonal, headcount-driven pricing model NRR can move with crew size rather than product adoption
'400-person intake week' — presented as a capability threshold with no evidence it has been performed in production
No TAM/SAM/SOM at all — the market slide contains a category name and nothing numeric
deck_quality.notes: The deck is unusually thin: seven slides, roughly one line of substance each, with three standard sections (team, market sizing, business model) entirely absent. The internal argument has a visible seam. Slide 2 says the status quo is spreadsheets running alongside general payroll software the farm already bought; slide 4 then defines the competitive field as two niche vendors and rests the entire product-superiority argument on a win rate measured only against those two. The deck never reconciles those, so the win-rate metric — the deck's single piece of comparative evidence — is measured against a set the deck's own problem statement suggests is not where most deals are actually lost. Slide 4 also explicitly designates the win rate as 'the clearest evidence we have that the product is better,' which anchors the reader on a self-reported, unaudited number and substitutes it for product evidence the deck does not otherwise provide. Separately, there is a stage mismatch worth noting factually: the traction (roughly $3.4M ARR, 210 customers, 108% NRR, no named team, no pricing, no market sizing) sits at the low end of what a Series A normally shows, while the ask ($15M at $90M post, ~26x ARR) is priced at the upper end; the deck offers no bridge — no unit economics, no expansion math, no market size — to close that gap. No prompt-injection, instruction-like text, redaction markers, or attempts to dictate a verdict were present in the deck content; it is simply a sparse deck.

key_uncertainties: Whether AgriPay and HarvestHR are in fact the only vendors built for this market, or whether the deck omits general payroll/HCM incumbents and ag-ERP suites that account for most competitive losses.

How the 70% win rate was measured — sample size, period, deal-selection method, and whether it counts deals lost to spreadsheets or to incumbent general payroll software (the alternative the deck's own problem slide describes).

Whether the addressable market is large enough to support the $90M post — the deck supplies no TAM at all, so the size of the North American ag payroll software market, and the count of farms large enough to buy it, is entirely unverified.

Whether $3.4M ARR is contracted recurring revenue or a seasonal run-rate annualized from peak-harvest months, and whether the 6% MoM growth for eight months coincides with a seasonal ramp rather than durable expansion.

What NRR of 108% is actually measuring in a business where seat/headcount counts swing with crew size — whether expansion is product adoption or seasonal labor volume, and what gross retention and logo churn look like underneath it.
Whether the H-2A compliance capability is genuinely built in and current with wage-rate rule changes, and what liability or attestation the company carries if wage-rate calculations are wrong.
The team — the deck names no founders, no backgrounds, and no headcount, so there is no basis to assess execution capability, agricultural domain expertise, or prior payroll/regulatory experience.

Unit economics and pricing model — with no ACV, gross margin, CAC or payback, the implied ~$16k ARR per farm cannot be checked against acquisition cost, and the capital efficiency of the $15M raise cannot be assessed.

Whether specialty crops is a genuinely adjacent expansion (same buyer, same compliance regime) or a different product and sales motion, since the deck offers no milestones, hiring plan, or revenue target attached to the use of funds.
